vignette:
I first met Raj in my office during a cool autumn afternoon. He is a fifty-year-old South Asian man, a husband, and a father of two-a boy now twelve and a girl who is nine. He is an animator by trade, a man who spends his days crafting fluid, beautiful motion from static frames. He tells me this is ironic, because for the last three years, his own life has felt frozen.

The trauma began in the spring of 2020. His daughter, Priya, then six years old, began to complain of persistent headaches and a strange, unshakable fatigue. Raj and his wife, Anjali, took her to the pediatrician, then to a specialist, then to the emergency room. The diagnosis came like a physical blow: a brain tumor. Malignant. The weeks that followed were a blur of white hospital walls, the beeping of monitors, and the sterile smell of antiseptic. Raj remembers the exact moment the neurosurgeon spoke to them in a quiet conference room. He remembers the way the doctor's mouth moved, forming words like "resection" and "prognosis," but the sounds seemed to arrive a full second after the lips finished moving, as if he were watching a badly dubbed film.

He stayed by Priya's bedside for seventeen days straight. He barely ate. He stopped sleeping. He would watch her chest rise and fall under the thin hospital blanket, counting each breath, terrified that one would be the last. He began to develop a ritual: every time a nurse entered the room, he would mentally scan the room for the nearest exit. Every time the heart monitor beeped irregularly, his own heart would seize, and he would feel a wave of heat wash over his body, followed by a cold, clammy dread.

Priya survived. The surgery was successful. The chemotherapy was grueling, but she is now in remission. Her hair has grown back. She laughs again. She goes to school. To the outside world, the crisis is over.

But for Raj, the crisis has never ended.

He tells me he cannot sit in a quiet room anymore. The silence feels like a held breath, a prelude to bad news. He now works from home exclusively, hunched over his drawing tablet in a corner of his bedroom. He can no longer animate scenes of children playing or families reuniting. The sight of a child running in a park-a scene he once drew with joy-now makes his throat tighten. He finds himself drawing the same frame over and over: a hospital room, a single bed, a dim light. He deletes it, draws it again, deletes it.

He has become a man of hypervigilance. At night, he walks the hallways of his home, checking the locks three times. He calls his daughter's school every morning to confirm she arrived safely. He has memorized the shortest route to the nearest hospital from every location in the city. When his wife suggests they plan a vacation, he feels a surge of panic so intense he has to excuse himself to the bathroom to breathe.

The worst moments come without warning. A car horn. The smell of hand sanitizer. The sight of a child's crayon drawing left on the kitchen table. These triggers send him spiraling into a dissociative state he describes as "watching my own life from the ceiling." He will be standing in the kitchen, and suddenly he is back in that hospital room, watching himself from above as a younger, terrified version of himself sits in a plastic chair, hands trembling.

He has not slept through the night in three years. He wakes at 3:17 AM every morning-the exact time Priya's first surgery began-drenched in sweat, heart pounding, convinced he has heard a monitor flatline. He lies there, rigid, until the sun comes up, rehearsing the names of every medication she took, every dosage, every side effect.

His marriage has become a landscape of silences. Anjali has tried to reach him, to tell him that their daughter is fine, that they can move on. But Raj cannot move on. He feels that if he stops worrying, if he lowers his guard, the universe will punish him. The worry has become his shield. The vigilance has become his love.

He is a man who once made a living creating the illusion of life. Now, he is trapped in a single, frozen frame, unable to advance the story, unable to let the next scene begin.
